# Results — Study 141 (Turnover-Anomaly) on real S&P 500 data

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Turnover signal = annual
trading volume (yfinance, daily → annual sum) ÷ weighted-average diluted shares outstanding
(EDGAR 10-K, shared cache). Sanity filter applied: 0.1 ≤ turnover ≤ 50 (removes unit-error
artefacts from the EDGAR cache, ~2% of firm-years). Signal year y → forward returns in
calendar year y+1 (one-year lag). Universe: current S&P 500 members projected back
(**survivorship-biased** — results are upper bounds on any live edge). As-of **2026-06-14**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Coverage | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|
| EDGAR shares outstanding | fiscal years 2008–2024, 412 tickers | shared cache |
| yfinance annual volume | calendar years 2007–2025, 412 tickers | `e9d355a67b97` |
| Annual returns (yrret) | calendar years 2009–2025 (fwd ret from signal years 2008–2024) | shared cache |

Signal years used: **2008–2024** (17 years). Low-coverage 2007 excluded. 2025 excluded
because its forward year (2026) is incomplete as of the run date.

Average valid tickers per signal year: **~355** (ranges from 220 in 2008 to 402 in 2024).

## The quintile sort — turnover vs next-year returns

Each year, stocks are sorted into five equal-count quintiles by annual turnover (Q1 = lowest,
Q5 = highest). Returns are the equal-weight average of the quintile's next-year price change.

| Quintile | Median turnover | Mean next-year return |
|---|--:|--:|
| **Q1 — low turnover** | ~1.1× | **+15.3%** |
| Q2 | ~1.6× | +15.3% |
| Q3 | ~2.1× | +17.2% |
| Q4 | ~2.7× | +18.9% |
| **Q5 — high turnover** | ~7.8× | **+28.2%** |
| Equal-weight market | — | +19.0% |

**Direction reversed vs the published claim.** In this survivorship-biased S&P 500 sample,
**high-turnover names dramatically outperform** low-turnover names (Q5 +28.2% vs Q1 +15.3%),
the exact opposite of Datar-Naik-Radcliffe (1998). Low-turnover stocks (Q1) *underperform*
the market by −3.7%/yr.

## Statistical tests

### Hedge (Q1 low-turnover minus market)

| n | mean | vol | Sharpe | HAC *t* | hit rate |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 17 | **−3.7%/yr** | 4.7% | −0.80 | **−3.94** | 24% |

The Q1-minus-market hedge is **significantly negative** (HAC *t* = −3.94, well beyond the |t|=2
inference bar). Low-turnover stocks reliably underperform the equal-weight index in this sample.

### Spread (Q1 minus Q5 — the "short high, long low" Datar trade)

| n | mean | vol | Sharpe | HAC *t* | hit rate |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 17 | **−12.9%/yr** | 13.3% | −0.97 | **−4.75** | 18% |

The long-low / short-high spread loses **−12.9%/yr** with HAC *t* = −4.75. The Datar-Naik-Radcliffe
trade, taken at face value on these names, **loses strongly**. It wins in only 3 of 17 years (18%).

### Shuffled-label control

The shuffled-label null (500 draws, random quintile assignment each year) produces a
Q1-market mean of **+0.01%** (essentially zero), confirming that the real result is
driven by the signal's ranking, not by the portfolio-construction mechanic.

The real Q1−market (−3.7%) is **far below** the shuffle mean (+0.01%), confirming that
the low-turnover end genuinely underperforms — but in the *wrong direction* for the claim.

## Interpretation

The strong, statistically significant result in the **opposite direction** of the original
finding has two primary explanations:

1. **Survivorship bias (dominant).** The EDGAR panel contains only firms that survived
   into the current S&P 500. High-turnover stocks that failed (fell off the index) are
   excluded. The high-turnover quintile is systematically populated by *the winners*: NVDA
   (GPU boom), AMZN (e-commerce), NFLX (streaming) — all current S&P 500 members with
   extreme trailing volume. Their survivorship creates an upward-biased return, not a live
   tradable edge.

2. **Momentum co-movement.** In the recent period (2017–2024), the largest-cap, most-traded
   names substantially outperformed. High turnover in this era proxies for market-cap weight
   and momentum exposure, both positive-return factors in the sample period.

The original Datar-Naik-Radcliffe (1998) effect (high turnover underperforms) was documented
on a broader, non-survivorship-biased universe across 1963–1991. On today's S&P 500 survivor
set in a momentum-driven 2008–2024 sample, the relationship inverts.

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** The turnover signal is strongly statistically significant (HAC |t| ≥ 3.9
  on both the hedge and the spread), but **directionally reversed** vs the published claim.
  The signal is real in this sample but contradicts the hypothesis: the Datar-Naik-Radcliffe
  "high-turnover underperforms" claim is **not supported** — it reverses. The likely driver is
  survivorship bias, not a new alpha.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The signal inverts the literature's claim; the mechanical
  implementation of the "long low, short high" Datar trade loses −12.9%/yr (HAC *t* = −4.75).
  Even "going the other way" (long high-turnover) is not tradable because it is driven by
  concentrated bets on surviving winners known only in hindsight.
- **Survivorship check — NOT SUPPORTED.** The S&P 500 survivorship bias dominates the result
  and prevents any honest estimate of the true live edge.
